mn95:2.1: Satussada—populous: literally, according to Comy, should be ‘beset by beings’.
mn95:8.2: ‘It is not proper that you go to see the monk Gotama’ (na arahati ... upasaṅkamituṁ): a peculiar idiomatic use of arahati. ‘Vuddhasīlī—mature in virtue’: this meaning of vuddha (=vaḍḍha, ‘increased’, according to Comy) is unusual.
mn95:9.14: Vigatacāpalla—rid of vacillation: rendered by some as merely ‘fickleness’, but according to Comy this is not quite right; cf. Vbh. 351.
mn95:9.15: That intentional actions do have results. ‘What is bad for the brahmin race’ was to hold annihilationist and acausal views, as some other teachers did.
mn95:9.19: ‘Gone for refuge for life’ (pāṇehi saraṇaṁ gato): compare the more usual idiom pāṇupetaṁ saraṇaṁ gataṁ.
mn95:12.11: The young brahmin is contesting the Buddha’s authority in matters of Dhamma by affirming the correctness of the brahminical religious tradition enshrined in the Vedas. Itihitiha-paramparāya piṭaka-sampadāya—handed down by oral tradition, generation after generation, coming down in the scriptures.
mn95:12.12: The brahmins come to a dogmatic, exclusive conclusion about the truth of their tradition.
mn95:13.4: Kāpaṭika has to admit that such a claim is dogmatic and not based on ‘knowing and seeing’, which means insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā).
mn95:13.9: The hymns (manta) means the Vedic hymns, as in the Rig Veda and so on.
mn95:14.1: An orally-transmitted tradition of hymns which brahmins believed to be divinely inspired.
mn95:14.5: Diṭṭhinijjhānakkhanti—acceptance of a view after pondering it: together with its parallel dhammanijjhānakkhanti (‘acceptance of a teaching after pondering it’, used from section 26 onward), this expression is difficult to render precisely; it denotes provisionally accepting a view or teaching on reflection, short of direct knowledge.
mn95:20.2: ‘He places his faith in him’ (tamhi saddhaṁ niveseti): this idiom is interesting in its connection with abhinivisati (to insist on, or to interpret) and the Commentarial use of abhinivesa as ‘interpretation’ preceding knowledge.
mn95:28.3: Dhamma here means a teaching, or simply ‘the Dhamma’.
mn95:34.12: Brahmins reckoned themselves to be the offspring of Brahmā's (the Kinsman’s) head; low-caste workers were thought to be the product of his feet.
